Hidden addiction

The Functioning Alcoholic: When Everything Looks Fine from the Outside

He works, pays the bills, never seems truly drunk. But the family sees what the world doesn't.

Steven H. White · approximately 8 min read

“‘Functioning’ lasts as long as the body can take it. The body doesn't negotiate.”

Important: after long, regular drinking, stopping suddenly can be dangerous. Withdrawal can cause seizures and delirium. If your partner wants to stop, it should not be overnight and alone, but with medical support.

“But he goes to work.” It's one of the most common things family members tell themselves. He shows up, does his job, pays the bills. He isn't lying in the street, he hasn't lost his job. He's not like a “real” alcoholic.

The trouble is, the picture of the “real” alcoholic most of us carry around is the late, visible stage of the illness. Most of addiction happens before that, quietly, behind a tidy exterior.

From the inside: the cost of functioning

On the outside, I functioned

Someone once asked me how I went so long without getting caught. How nobody noticed. I gave him an example, and it made him think.

Say you go into work in the morning, somewhere between 7 and 9. A colleague comes by, says good morning, sometimes compliments you, sometimes has a coffee with you, sometimes not. He has good moods and bad moods, and then the work, the shift, carries on. That's just how he is.

We don't know whether he's got four beers or three shots in him right now. That's how we're used to him. If he's an alcoholic, he takes care of the smell, but his face, the way he moves, the way he says hello are all the same as always. That's what normal looks like. Nobody starts from the assumption that a colleague has already been drinking that morning. He's a minor character in our lives, and we never see the real things.

I functioned. Nobody thought I was driving drunk. In the mornings I'd stop at two bars, and then I'd do my job.

It's logical: the closer someone is to me, the harder it is to hide it from them. You have to lie to them more, manipulate them more. Because I didn't admit there was a problem. All I saw was that people were getting at me and nagging me.

I think most breakthroughs come for two reasons. The first: when the substance we love stops giving and starts taking. That moment comes in everyone's life. We get used to it, and it starts to shrink the pleasure, the reward. I got used to it too, and it kept getting worse.

The second runs alongside it. You feel like you've hardly had anything, so you drink more, but meanwhile the balance shifts. I was no longer a twenty-year-old stallion, but a working husband, thirty-three and dead tired from the kid. Of course I couldn't handle as much anymore. Then came the physical symptoms, feeling sick.

That's how it turns around in an instant. In the last years I was already terrified of drinking. Nobody saw that, of course. A day and a half without a drink was enough, and my body warned me with an epileptic seizure. It wasn't epilepsy. It was withdrawal, deciding my fate.

One thing I know for sure: my body didn't stay quiet. Six bouts of pancreatitis, two seizures, one delirium. That's the 6+2+1.

“Functioning” lasts as long as the body can take it, and the body doesn't negotiate.

Five myths about the “functioning” alcoholic

1. “He works, so there's no problem.”
Work is often the last area where addiction starts to show. People do everything to keep things in order there, because work brings the money, the status and the alibi. The price gets paid elsewhere: at home, in the evenings, on weekends, in relationships.

2. “He's never really drunk.”
Some people don't drink a lot at once, but in small amounts throughout the day, keeping a steady level. From the outside they never seem drunk, but they're never fully sober either. That's exactly why it's so hard to notice.

3. “He only drinks beer.”
Beer seems more harmless than spirits. It's easy to explain and goes down quickly. But the body doesn't care what form the alcohol arrives in. If someone drinks it by the case, the percentage no longer matters.

4. “He never drinks in the morning.”
Many people think morning drinking is the line. If someone only drinks in the evening, that's still okay. But the question isn't when, it's whether he can go without. If skipping the evening drink brings irritability, restlessness and a bad mood, that tells you more than the time of day. What you don't see isn't necessarily not happening.

5. “If something were wrong, the doctor would have said so.”
A doctor sees what they're told and what the tests show. Someone who is dependent rarely says honestly how much they drink. The physical consequences often only become obvious once things are already serious.

“Functioning” doesn't mean there's no problem. It means someone else is carrying it.

What the family sees and the world doesn't

Living with a functioning alcoholic often means being alone with what you know. Colleagues, friends, sometimes even relatives say there's nothing wrong, he's doing fine. To a colleague, he's just a minor character they're used to. But you're close, and you see:

that the evenings revolve more and more around drinking;
that the rhythm of the weekends has changed;
that he's more irritable when he can't drink;
that there's always alcohol at shared plans, or if there isn't, he's in a hurry to get home;
that more and more is left to you.

If you see this, you're not exaggerating. The fact that nobody outside notices doesn't mean there's nothing to notice. It means he hides it well, and that you're close to him. And that's why you also get the most lies.

Why is it harder to say out loud?

Because there's no clear moment you can point to. He hasn't lost his job, hasn't caused an accident, hasn't been in hospital. For every argument you have, there's a counterargument: “but he's functioning.”

That's exactly why it's worth not waiting for the big events. Nothing dramatic has to happen for you to have the right to worry. Your own experience, what you see day after day, is enough.

A few questions for yourself

How much time in a week goes by without him drinking at all?

How does he react when plans don't involve alcohol?

What have you taken on so that everything looks fine from the outside?

Who have you ever told about what you see?

If these questions were hard to answer, that isn't your weakness. It shows that behind the “functioning,” there's your work too.

Steven H. White - sober for ten years. His body kept count for him: 6+2+1.

Functioning is not the same as being well

A job, paid bills and a tidy exterior do not tell you what alcohol is costing the person or the family.

One thing to remember

You do not need a catastrophe to trust what you see.

Your day-to-day experience is enough reason to take your concern seriously.
